summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Danish national criminal law and document rules apply here; equality and family law are set locally.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was set at 18 and stayed there until 1988, when the Faroes adopted Denmark's gender-neutral age of 15, eleven years after Denmark made that change.

In November 2006 activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law matching the other Nordic countries. Neither existed at that date, and homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. A separate petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures. After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen an internet petition collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn added a further 2,000 by email and from collection points in shops, tourist centres and petrol stations.

The anti-discrimination provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last country in Northern Europe to ban discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. Anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the enumerated grounds, so a trans visitor or resident targeted as a member of a group falls outside the article as written, and no separate gender-identity hate-crime provision appears in the sources.

The most fully documented anti-LGBT attack is the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen, an openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host, who was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police declined to handle the case because no Faroese law at the time banned discrimination against sexual minorities. The source records that he was later admitted to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression worsened by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men in Tórshavn intent on physically assaulting them; the group noted that nowhere else had it been attacked.

Public visibility has drawn sustained opposition. The first gay pride march, in 2005, provoked much controversy. In June 2015 the Speaker of the Løgting, Jógvan á Lakjuni, published a letter to the editor attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as "non-culture". Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. In July 2015, two days before the national holiday, he demanded that Pride be banned, and the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. In September 2010 av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures, a visiting drag performance group and Pride events, and the documented actions are a refusal to sit at an official table, a letter to a newspaper and calls for a ban. No prosecution, conviction or official sanction under the 2007 provision appears in the sources. The two assaults on record date from 2005 and 2006; in the one case where the police response is documented, officers declined to act, and the legal footing that exists today covers sexual orientation and not gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Faroe Islands equality legislation arrived on a different timetable from the rest of the region. The territory was the last country in Northern Europe to criminalise discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and it matched the Nordic gender-neutral age of consent only in 1988, eleven years after Denmark. A visitor arriving from Denmark or another Nordic country meets a legal floor on sexual-orientation discrimination that is newer and narrower than the one at home.

Religiously motivated opposition to LGBT visibility is expressed openly by elected figures rather than confined to the margins: a party leader cited his religion when declining an official banquet, compared an LGBT organisation to whaling protesters and called for Pride to be banned, and a Speaker of the Løgting used a newspaper letter to attack the national broadcaster over its LGBT airtime and a drag performance.

Civil-society petitioning has been the recurring mechanism on the other side, from the 20,000 signatures of 2006 to the 2,000 collected in person after the Tórshavn assault. The petition against same-sex marriage, at 1,262 signatures, shows the counter-current in the same period.

The sources record no case brought under the provision that took effect on 1 January 2007, so its use in practice is not established.

Petitioning has been the main civic instrument available to residents: around 20,000 signatures in 2006 for a discrimination ban and a registered-partnership law, 1,262 against same-sex marriage, and a combined 22,000 gathered online and in person after the 2006 assault.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory holds no figures on trans-specific violence in the Faroe Islands. The two assaults it records involve an openly gay man and a visiting drag performance group, and no general homicide or violent-crime rate is provided, so no magnitude can be attached to either and no comparison against background violence can be made.

Enforcement of the 1 January 2007 anti-discrimination provision is not documented. No prosecution, conviction or complaint outcome appears in the sources, and the practical reach of the article toward statements targeting trans people is unresolved.

Document and gender-marker rules specific to the Faroe Islands were not identified in the inventory; Danish national document rules govern here and are carried by the parent record. No information was found on trans-specific healthcare, facility access, or police and border practice toward trans visitors.

No hate-crime aggravation covering gender identity appears in the sources. The criminal penalties identified attach only to the enumerated grounds of the anti-discrimination article, and the recorded political and public-order disputes concern sexual orientation and drag performance rather than trans identity as such.
